summary:
We developed **Fieldshift**, a decision-support web tool that helps farmers choose smarter crop rotations using NASA Earth observation data. Farmers enter their field's soil, water access, and crop history, then set their own priorities — conserving water, building soil fertility, reducing erosion, market income, and breaking pest cycles. Fieldshift compares at least three rotation strategies, including the farmer's current rotation as a baseline, scoring each against those priorities and explaining the supporting evidence drawn from datasets like SMAP, ECOSTRESS, GPM, Landsat/MODIS, NASA POWER, and GRACE/GRACE-FO, alongside the potential benefits, risks, and open information gaps.

This directly addresses the challenge: translating NASA's long-term environmental data into practical, farmer-friendly rotation insights that strengthen soil health and resilience to shifting weather and water conditions. It matters because farmers worldwide are making high-stakes planting decisions with less predictable rainfall, declining soil health, and growing water scarcity, often without access to the long-term data needed to plan ahead. Fieldshift is explicitly built to support — not replace — farmer judgment and local agricultural expertise, surfacing patterns and trade-offs worth discussing, while always flagging where human review is needed.
details:
While the deploy finishes in the background, here’s the detailed write-up for that section:

How it works

Fieldshift is a client-side web app. A farmer fills in a farm profile (soil, drainage, water access, crop history) and sets five priority sliders (water conservation, soil fertility, erosion control, market income, pest-cycle breaking). The app then scores four rotation strategies — including the farmer’s current rotation as an explicit baseline — against those priorities using a transparent, inspectable weighting formula (not a black-box model), and shows each strategy’s supporting evidence, benefits, risks, and open information gaps side by side, plus a radar chart for an at-a-glance trade-off comparison. A separate illustrative field-map view lets users drag rainfall/temperature sliders to see how erosion, water-stress, and frost-risk zones might shift.

Benefits & intended impact

It turns NASA’s long-term environmental record into a decision aid a farmer can actually act on in minutes, instead of needing geospatial expertise to interpret raw satellite data. The intended impact is better-informed rotation choices in regions facing water scarcity and soil decline — reducing bare-field erosion, nitrogen-fertilizer dependence, and water waste over time, while explicitly deferring final judgment to the farmer and local agronomists.

Tools & stack

Plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript (no framework) — deliberately lightweight so it loads fast and works without a backend. The radar chart and field-risk grid are hand-built in SVG, no charting library. State persists client-side via localStorage. Hosted as a static site on GitHub Pages and Netlify, version-controlled on GitHub. For supporting materials, I used Playwright (headless Chromium) for high-resolution screenshots and PDF slide export, ffmpeg with Microsoft Edge’s free text-to-speech for a narrated demo video, and Claude Code as an AI pair-programmer throughout development and deployment.

Creativity

Rather than exposing raw satellite variables, the design translates them into priorities a farmer already thinks in. The scoring is fully explainable — every number traces back to a visible crop attribute and dataset — and every strategy card is honest about its own risks and data gaps instead of presenting a single “best” answer with false confidence.

Factors we weighed

Explainability over prediction accuracy, accessibility for non-technical users (a glossary explains terms like NDVI and evapotranspiration), honesty about what’s illustrative sample data versus real NASA API integration, and keeping the farmer and local expert firmly in the loop rather than automating them out of the decision.
